title: The White House needs a ground stop
subtitle: On Still Counting EP13, we discussed a chaotic Friday the 13th and a White House that hasn’t learned anything from the midterms.
contentHtml:
Buckle your seatbelts, because Galen, Clare, and I got a little more wound up than usual on this week’s Still Counting, where we discussed the Nvidia story/scandal and the nationwide ground stop on Friday, just the second since Sept. 11. It’s hard not to feel that way when the Secretary of Transportation has trouble explaining WTF was going on. It’s been a highly turbulent two weeks for the White House since the midterms, and with 793 more days remaining in President Trump’s term, we’re nowhere near our final descent into God-knows-what. Pressing for an analogy, I likened the current course to the prolonged and gory denouement of the movie The Substance.1

Video above, audio below. Like always, we appreciate any comments, likes, reviews and subscribes.

The context

Unless there’s another disruption around the holidays, the ground stop that the FAA ordered late Friday afternoon probably won’t be remembered as a seminal political event. And I don’t think it should be, although maybe I’d feel differently if I were stranded on the tarmac at LaGuardia at the time.

However, I think it represents an unusually clean natural experiment. Something serious but not that serious happened. It was unplanned, and the government needed to respond. It’s not something like the Nvidia story, which has incredibly wide-ranging implications and would be a communications challenge for any White House to deal with regardless of the president.

Instead, the communication surrounding the ground stop ought to have been fairly basic political blocking-and-tackling, a test of whether you’re executing your fundamentals. It’s also one of the first such tests after Democrats swept into power two weeks ago in an historic repudiation of President Trump. Is the White House making any adjustments to acknowledge that Americans are sick of how they’ve handled business?

I don’t have anything in particular against Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, although he doesn’t have any obvious qualifications for the job, having been: a nationally-recognized lumberjack, a Real World contestant, a sportscaster, a prosecutor and district attorney, a 5-term U.S. Representative from Wisconsin, a senior counsel for a lobbying firm, and a CNN and Fox News contributor. It’s kind of a fun resumé, but there’s not much obviously transit-related. (To be fair, the previous secretary of transportation, Pete Buttigieg, didn’t have many transportation-adjacent credentials either.)

But Trump presumably chose Duffy because he watches a lot of TV, and Duffy has been on TV a lot. He’s at least supposed to look and act the part.

I don’t want to turn Silver Bulletin into a #Resistance blog that chronicles every minor outrage of the Trump administration. But for some reason, I felt triggered by the press conference that Duffy and the Homeland Security Secretary, former Oklahoma Sen. Markwayne Mullin, held on Friday night:

I’m not a crisis communications expert, but I don’t think I need to be to describe what constitutes blocking-and-tackling in this sort of situation:

  • Clearly explain what happened

  • Reassure people that they’re safe, or if they’re not safe, what you’re doing to make them safe

  • Own some acceptable fraction of the blame

  • Present an image of competence and professionalism

  • Avoid overly politicizing the situation, especially when it comes to a system like aviation safety that is intrinsically nonpartisan.

I’m a very frequent flier, and — possibly unpopular opinion — I think the U.S. aviation system mostly does an outstanding job.2 But I think Duffy and Mullin deserve a failing grade for this press conference.

There were a dozen or so references to President Trump, praising a Dear Leader whose party just lost Senate seats in Kansas, Alaska, South Carolina, Texas, and Mississippi.

There was also extensive lobbying by Duffy (and, to a lesser extent, Mullin) for new ATC funding. I don’t have any particular opinion about this — as a taxpayer, I can imagine worse expenditures than modernizing air-traffic control — though it might be noted that the Trump Administration made a big pretense of starving government during the aborted DOGE era.

What really bothered me, though, is that Duffy and Mullin almost went out of their way to not make it clear what in the hell was going on.

They explained, I guess, the what of what was happening but not the how or the why. Imagine a friend texts you to tell you his car just got totaled. “Holy shit bro what happened,” you respond. “Well, the front right side got smashed to pieces, and the airbag deployed,” he answers. “And that’s just the start of it tbh. I might be in the market for a new ride 😂.”

You might make various inferences from this — my inference would be that the crash was my friend’s fault — but either way, this isn’t a responsive answer. It’s obfuscatory. The friend doubled down on precisely what happened, but there was conspicuously no why.

I don’t think there’s any deep conspiracy behind Friday’s ground stop, and I’m glad, I guess, the FAA exercised an abundance of caution in calling for one. It doesn’t seem like any of the more salacious explanations — terrorists, hackers, or rogue AI agents — had anything to do with it. Although who knows: Mullin later went on Hannity and cited an anonymous Silicon Valley source who said that “SI” might in fact be responsible for the recent series of weird outages and disruptions.

But at the presser, Mullin and Duffy couldn’t really keep their story straight. Upon questioning, Mullin did provide what seemed like a relatively straightforward answer 15 minutes in:3

So, let’s talk about the cybersecurity once again. We’re still looking at it; we’re not ruling out anything. What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology just wasn’t — it was overwhelming the older system, which is why Secretary Duffy made it very clear the patchwork doesn’t work.

So basically, Mullin said, the FAA installed some new software and/or hardware and then something broke. Hey, it happens. Once or twice a year during an election or sports season, we’ll discover some theretofore unknown problem with FLIPR or ELWAY. There’s only so much testing you can do in advance. It’s nevertheless embarrassing when this happens, although there also aren’t national security implications riding on whether we have the Broncos -2.5 or -3.5. This is more likely to happen when you’ve made some kind of recent change to the code, but as often as not, some preexisting bug surfaces only once certain conditions are met.

But Duffy side-eyed Mullin as he gave this explanation and, at one point, almost seemed to physically nudge him. Presumably, that’s because it undercut Duffy’s emphasis on old equipment becoming overloaded:

So, what happened, right? I've heard a lot of the rumors, like Markwayne has. But what we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system. I think every single one of your networks have covered the president and myself talking about this for the last two years. The president, for the last year, has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand-new air traffic control system. So, we have TDM telecom, so this is analog telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down. And — I shouldn't say they went down; they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down. Now, I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump. And our new IP switches did not go down; it's the old hardware that went down. And I think the question for the American people is, do you want your Congress to fund this?

Strictly speaking, you can square these explanations, sort of. Again, it wouldn’t be uncommon in something like FLIPR for us to add some new code and then, for any number of reasons, it breaks something in a pre-existing part of the model. But he’s obfuscating any role that the new equipment played, possibly because it’s hard to ask for more new toys when the one you just acquired sent the aviation system to a halt.

One thing I was curious about: are late afternoons on Friday some sort of “rush hour” for air traffic, when systems are particularly strained? Actually, sort of yes. There isn’t any particular S-tier peak for the number of planes in the air. (Notoriously busy travel days like the Sunday after Thanksgiving don’t necessarily feature more flights — which is what matters from an ATC standpoint — it’s just that the flights are fuller.) But based on BTS data, there are four busy days for air travel — Sundays, Mondays, Thursdays, and Fridays — and three slower ones (Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Saturdays).4

When is air traffic highest?

I also assumed that late afternoons might be some sort of lull in air traffic on the theory that it’s usually more logical to travel in the morning or the evening. But what matters for air traffic is the number of planes in the air at a given time, not when they depart — plus the United States spans several time zones. An 8 a.m. PT flight from SFO to Newark might be on its final approach by 3:30 ET, but it probably won’t have landed yet.

In a later explanation to the press, Duffy said the problems had in fact resulted from the installation of new equipment: installing a new router as part of a transition from copper to fiber-optic connections. I don’t have any particular reason to doubt this explanation, but he could have said it in the presser.

There was also a bit of narrative tension when Duffy and Mullin were asked questions along the lines of: if you say ATC needs $50 billion in new funding because the system is broken, how can you claim that Americans are safe now? I’m a touch more sympathetic to them on that point. I don’t think it’s inherently unreasonable for the Secretary of Transportation or the DHS Secretary to both reassure people and lobby for more funding. But I did think Duffy foregrounding the lobbying so much reflected an example of not “reading the room” or the mood well. Demonstrate that you’re on top of the problem first when there’s some sort of immediate crisis and you’ll build credibility to ask for more resources later.

I’ve seen some claims that this was the first nationwide ground stop since Sept. 11, but that isn’t true. There was also one in 2023. Here was Buttigieg briefing the press that morning:

I wouldn’t claim this to be some sort of master class in political communication — Buttigieg’s explanation of the causes is a little vague. But he’s getting the basic blocking and tackling right. We’re on the problem; safety is always our first priority, blah, blah, blah. There was no sycophantic praise for then-President Biden. There was some low-key effort to lobby Congress for more ATC funding, but Mayor Pete didn’t have the Shriners Telethon vibe that Duffy did. And Buttigieg was dressed in a suit.5 He didn’t insist on calling AI “SI” following Trump’s directive, as Mullin did, the sort of Republican equivalent of “Latinx,” a term that doesn’t have widespread adoption and could only serve to confuse people in the middle of a crisis.

Again, I’m not saying the ground stop on Friday was an especially important story. A lot of people discovered the charms of the Aerostay Hotel: Sioux Falls Regional Airport, but it wasn’t Hurricane Katrina.

Still, I think it’s a revealing story precisely because it isn’t all that high-stakes. Trump’s cabinet officials are acting like they’re speaking on behalf of a president who has a 73 percent approval rating, not 37 percent. They don’t come across as being especially competent or professional. Historically, midterms are not particularly predictive of the forthcoming presidential result, but that’s partly because the White House typically responds rationally to new information by pivoting to the center or trimming its sails. The White House conspicuously did not do that during Friday’s mini-crisis.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

There’s quite a lot going on at the site!

  • We’re hiring a full-time editor and a part-time developer. We’d encourage you to pass the job listing along if you know someone who might be a good fit. Applications are open through Dec. 18. We’ll review applications over the holidays, and start setting up some first-round interviews in early January.

  • As you’ve surely seen by now, we also launched a site redesign this week. We’re continuing to make refinements, but we very much appreciate your feedback. And if there’s anything that seems outright broken, please email us at silver.bulletin.customer.service@gmail.com including details like what browser you’re using and how the problems surfaced.

  • Our March Madness projections are our second-most popular feature, after our election models. And they’re powered by COOPER, our college basketball ratings system. Last year, we launched COOPER a week or two before the tournament. This year, we’re hoping to begin publishing them next month (December) instead, at least for the men’s ratings, in time for the start of the conference season. We have quite an ambitious list of feature improvements, though, so that could slip by a couple of weeks. They include things like accounting for roster turnover and recruitment, coaching and program expenditures, better handling of home-court advantage, accounting properly for team pace, and projecting future games and possibly even things like conference winners, final standings and a team’s likelihood of making the tournament. This is a few weeks away, so we’ll go into the lab and have more for you as we get closer to launch.

Silver Bulletin has never had a ground stop. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a subscriber.

1

Not necessarily the sort of movie you’d want to watch on a cross-country flight.

2

I’ll admit it’s easier when you fly a fair amount of business class and/or premium economy and/or have status on various airlines and/or pay for TSA Pre and CLEAR.

3

Emphasis mine.

4

It’s logical enough: Tuesday and Wednesday are the heart of the work week, and Saturday is the middle of the weekend, while the other days are in the transition boundary where people go from work to recreation or vice versa.

5

Maybe that’s a potshot at Duffy, who later said he wasn’t able to change wardrobe because he’d just gotten off a flight himself. He could have shown up in a Beavis-and-Butt-Head T as far as I care. But if you’re going to pull off the “I couldn’t change into a suit because I’m so on top of this problem that I couldn’t spare 5 minutes,” you ought to demonstrate that you’re actually on top of the problem rather than filibuster.
